en: *Huayan jing yiji*, Scroll One, composed by the śramaṇa Huiguang of Dajue Monastery.
Regarding the "Chapter on the Enlightenment of the Tathāgata’s Radiance":
this clarifies that the Tathāgata’s mental karma (*manas-karman*) consists of the wisdom and practice of transformation and instruction.
Obstruction is like radiance;
because it brings about clear understanding of conditions, it is called awakening.
Regarding the emission of light from the *cakra* mark within this chapter,
up to the emission of light from between the eyebrows at the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*),
these differences in rank are manifested according to the distinctions among those who practice in accordance with the wisdom of the Tathāgata’s own essence.
The distinct names of the bodhisattvas manifest the differences in their practices, virtues, and stages.
Within the scope illuminated by this light, the first part clarifies the manifestation of the actual reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of the world-system.
Next, the Buddha is explained because he possesses internal illumination regarding the true nature (*dharmatā*); thus, the Buddha is explained next.
Because he has realized dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) through actual awakening, the Bodhisattva is explained [next].
This clarifies that the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*) is situated at the beginning, while the world of the perfectly awakened wisdom (*samyak-saṃbuddha-jñāna*) is situated in the middle.
Regarding the latter [section] on the world of sentient beings, it clarifies the initial manifestation of the internal characteristics of the arising of cultivation through accumulation.
Following that, it first clarifies the individual bodhisattvas,
and subsequently the individual worlds.
The subsequent clarification regarding the Buddha elucidates the characteristics of the final, complete, and perfect cultivation that results in the attainment of reality.
Within this context of the Bodhisattva:
First, Mañjuśrī is explained as such because he is the one who first realized the fundamental sublime wisdom of the true nature of *prajñā*.
Next, Samantabhadra is explained as such.
Because he is internally enlightened and externally radiant, he is called "Foremost in Enlightenment" (Bodhimukha).
Possessing this luminous clarity of awakening and illumination,
he is thus able to gather the myriad practices.
Because it possesses the merit of providing support, it is called the "Foremost Wealth.
Since it possesses the practice of gathering and assisting, it can provide inexhaustible benefit and profit;
because it yields the supreme benefits of world-transcendence, it is called the "Foremost Jewel."
Because he possesses inexhaustible resources and moisture,
he is able to fully perfect the virtues of benefiting both himself and others; therefore,
he is called "The Foremost in Virtue."
Since he is already endowed with complete virtue,
yet unless one possesses the skillful means of Prajñā to discern all things without omission, one cannot thoroughly understand conditions;
therefore, it next says "the Eye-Head."
Since one is no longer deluded once conditions have arisen, one is able to realize the merit of "daily renewal";
therefore, next, diligence is clarified as the foremost [of the perfections].
Since the method of daily renewal exists, there is no practice that is not accumulated.
Next, the "Dharma-Head" (Dharmottara) is explained.
Since all dharmas have been fully assembled, their true fusion radiates with brilliant light, illuminating everything without obstruction;
therefore, next, the "Wisdom-Head" (Jñānottara) is explained.
Because he possesses clear illumination that is unimpeded,
and because he is able to fully perfect the Way through goodness, compliance, harmony, and gentleness,
the "Worthy Leader" (Bhadramukha) is explained next.
Why are they all called "foremost" (*śreṣṭha*)?
It is because one wishes to clarify that they are the most excellent among the practices cultivated in the world;
since the worldly path reaches its ultimate fulfillment therein, they are called "foremost."
Furthermore, it is called "the beginning" because it marks the initial stage of cultivating and gathering the True Path.
Within this context, the emission of light first illuminates the trichiliocosm and ultimately reaches hundreds of thousands of billions of worlds.
This is intended to clarify that the initial arising is itself the characteristic of understanding;
furthermore, the reason for repeatedly mentioning the "east" in both proximate and remote contexts is the same as the explanation provided previously.
Furthermore, the statement that there is a great bodhisattva in each direction is intended to clarify the causal practices of the essential nature within skillful means (*upāya*).
The phrase "each having bodhisattvas as their retinue" [is likewise explained].
It is clear that there are no practices not subsumed [within this].
That each has come here signifies the perfect realization of the fruit-practice within one's own essence.
That Mañjuśrī is the foremost indicates that [the path] begins with the wondrous reality.
Furthermore, the reason one ultimately reaches the stage of Bhadramukha is...
To clarify that although this practice is profound and vast, its fulfillment occurs within the world, it is called "Worthy Head" (Bhadramukha).
Furthermore, practice does not exist in isolation;
it must rely upon objects to arise.
Therefore it is said that one begins with the golden color and culminates in the color of reality (tathatā).
Since there is a real accord with the mind, one thereby attains true awakening from within;
hence it is said that one purifies the Brahma-conduct in the presence of all Buddhas.
The reason why "first clarifying the wisdom of immovability" is stated is to clarify the original source from which true awakening first arises;
"finally reaching the subduing of the enemy" refers to the ultimate attainment.
It also clarifies that accomplishment exists within the world because it has not yet been manifested; it is precisely through detachment that one subdues resentment.

As for why Mañjuśrī speaks of his own accord without being questioned, it is because he wishes to clarify that wondrous eloquence arises from the Middle Way and does not depend on external conditions.
Furthermore, it clarifies the "uninvited friend.
If we speak in terms of receiving benefit,
this chapter elucidates the practice of seeking to hear the Dharma.
The lower grade clarifies the practice of seeking the teaching of the Dharma.
When discussing the sequence of the arising of conditions for this practice,
it is because the sublime reality must correspond to skillful means.
This refers to what Mañjuśrī has taught.
Since the provisional means have been clarified as being in accord with reality, this is the virtue of the means.
Thus, by means of this virtue, one matures and returns to the source, responding once again to reality.
The following clarifies the Chapter on Difficulties.
In this section, Mañjuśrī poses questions and the various bodhisattvas provide answers;
then, the various bodhisattvas pose questions and Mañjuśrī again provides answers.
Because he wishes to clarify that when the virtues are matured, they return to their source,
he manifests the Bodhisattva’s inquiry;
for it is by means of the source that all virtues are subsumed.
To manifest [the truth] perfectly and in accordance with reality is called answering.
